questions.question: What is a mesh in 3D graphics?
options: A collection of pixels forming an image
A collection of vertices, edges, and faces defining a 3D shape
A type of texture map for surfaces
A lighting model for rendering
questions.explanation: A mesh is the 3D wireframe structure made of vertices (points in space), edges (connections between vertices), and faces (polygons) that defines an object's shape.

questions.question: In PBR (Physically Based Rendering), what does the metalness property control?
options: How shiny the surface is
How heavy the object appears
Whether the surface behaves like a conductor (metal) or dielectric (plastic/ceramic)
The thickness of the object's edges
questions.explanation: Metalness (0 to 1) determines whether a surface is a conductor or dielectric. Metals reflect their tint color, while dielectrics (plastic, wood, skin) have white-tinted specular highlights.

questions.question: What is UV mapping in 3D?
options: A type of camera projection for ultraviolet light
A coordinate system (U=horizontal, V=vertical) for applying 2D textures to 3D surfaces
A method for computing vertex normals
A compression format for texture images
questions.explanation: UV mapping flattens a 3D mesh's surface into 2D space using U (horizontal) and V (vertical) coordinates. This tells the renderer which part of a texture image maps to each polygon.

questions.question: Which light type emits parallel rays from a fixed direction, like sunlight?
options: Point light
Spot light
Area light
Directional light
questions.explanation: A directional light emits rays that are perfectly parallel, simulating an infinitely distant source like the sun. Its position in the scene doesn't matter — only its direction.

questions.question: What is a normal map used for?
options: Setting the base color of a surface
Controlling reflection sharpness
Faking fine surface detail (bumps, scratches) without adding real geometry
Adjusting the roughness of a material
questions.explanation: A normal map stores per-pixel surface direction data in an RGB texture. By altering how light hits each pixel, it creates the illusion of bumps, dents, and scratches without any additional polygons.
